items.followUp: Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Identifies prokaryotic organization and its defining feature.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound, true nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming prokaryotic cells and stating that they lack a true nucleus.

rubric.why: Shows where the genetic material is found in a prokaryotic cell.
rubric.description: Their DNA lies in a nucleoid region in the cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for locating the DNA in the nucleoid or describing it as naked DNA in the cytoplasm.

rubric.why: Provides a correct example of a prokaryote.
rubric.description: Bacteria are prokaryotic organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example such as bacteria.

rubric.why: Identifies eukaryotic organization and its defining feature.
rubric.description: Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound, true nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming eukaryotic cells and stating that they have a true nucleus.

rubric.why: Distinguishes eukaryotic cellular organization from prokaryotic organization.
rubric.description: Eukaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning membrane-bound organelles; a correct eukaryotic example may be used to illustrate this type.

modelAnswer: Cells show two main types of cellular organization: prokaryotic and eukaryotic.
Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound, true nucleus; their DNA lies in a nucleoid region in the cytoplasm.
Bacteria are examples of prokaryotic organisms.
Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound, true nucleus.
They also contain membrane-bound organelles; plants, animals and fungi are made of eukaryotic cells.

items.followUp: Explain how root hairs help a plant absorb water and mineral salts.

rubric.why: Identifies how roots are adapted for absorption.
rubric.description: Root hairs provide a large surface area for absorption from the soil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking root hairs with increased absorptive surface area.

rubric.why: States the process by which water enters root cells.
rubric.description: Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming osmosis as the process of water uptake.

rubric.why: States the process used to take up mineral ions.
rubric.description: Mineral ions are absorbed by root cells by active transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming active transport for mineral-ion uptake.

rubric.why: Recognizes that active uptake requires energy.
rubric.description: Active transport uses energy to move ions, often against their concentration gradient.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that energy is required for active transport or that ions can be taken up against their concentration gradient.

modelAnswer: Root hairs provide a large surface area in contact with the soil.
Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis.
Mineral ions are absorbed by root cells by active transport, which requires energy.
Water and ions pass through the root tissues to the xylem for transport through the plant.

items.followUp: Explain the rules of binomial nomenclature and give two scientific names.

rubric.why: Explains why common names can cause confusion.
rubric.description: Common names vary between languages and regions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that common names are not uniform across languages or regions.

rubric.why: Explains the practical problem caused by variable common names.
rubric.description: The same organism may have different common names, or one common name may refer to different organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a resulting naming confusion.

rubric.why: States the advantage of scientific names.
rubric.description: Scientific names provide a standardized name used internationally for each species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that scientific names are standardized or universal.

rubric.why: Gives the essential structure of a scientific name.
rubric.description: Each scientific name consists of two words: the genus name followed by the species name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the two parts in the correct order.

rubric.why: Illustrates scientific naming with a correct example.
rubric.description: A correct scientific name illustrates the binomial system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least one correct scientific name, such as Homo sapiens or Mangifera indica.

modelAnswer: Common names vary from one language or region to another, so they may cause confusion.
The same organism may have different common names, and a common name may sometimes be used for different organisms.
Scientists therefore use scientific names, which are standardized internationally.
In binomial nomenclature, each scientific name has two words: the genus name followed by the species name.
For example, the scientific name of humans is Homo sapiens, and that of mango is Mangifera indica.

items.followUp: Describe the role of carbon dioxide and water in photosynthesis, and write the word equation.

rubric.why: Explains the role of chlorophyll.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll absorbs light.

rubric.why: Explains why light is needed.
rubric.description: Light supplies the energy needed for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying light as the energy source for photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Explains the conversion of energy during the process.
rubric.description: The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy stored in food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing conversion of light energy into chemical energy.

rubric.why: States the useful product made using the absorbed energy.
rubric.description: The chemical energy is used to make glucose (food) from carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying glucose or food as the product made in photosynthesis.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in green plants absorbs light energy.
Light provides the energy required for photosynthesis.
The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy.
This energy is used to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

items.followUp: Describe the structure of a chloroplast and state the functions of its main parts.

rubric.why: Describes the chloroplast's outer structure.
rubric.description: A plastid is enclosed by a double membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that plastids have a double membrane.

rubric.why: Identifies the internal fluid region of a chloroplast.
rubric.description: The internal fluid matrix is called the stroma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the stroma.

rubric.why: Identifies the chlorophyll-containing internal membrane structures.
rubric.description: Thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana and contain chlorophyll.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming grana or thylakoids.

rubric.why: Names a plastid type and its function.
rubric.description: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing chloroplast function.

rubric.why: Names and describes the functions of other plastid types.
rubric.description: Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments; leucoplasts are colourless and store food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly pairing chromoplasts with pigments/colour or leucoplasts with food storage.

modelAnswer: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in plant cells and are enclosed by a double membrane.
A chloroplast contains a fluid matrix called the stroma.
Its internal membrane sacs, called thylakoids, are arranged in stacks called grana and contain chlorophyll.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; chromoplasts contain coloured pigments that give colour to plant parts.
Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food such as starch, oils or proteins.

items.followUp: Name two biological problems faced by people today and briefly state their effects.

rubric.why: Identifies major biological issues.
rubric.description: Examples include food shortage, disease, energy shortage and environmental pollution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming two relevant biological issues.

rubric.why: Recognizes additional major biological issues.
rubric.description: Examples include food shortage, disease, energy shortage and environmental pollution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two further relevant issues, or for clearly explaining the importance of the named issues.

modelAnswer: Major biological issues today include food shortage, disease, energy shortage and environmental pollution.
These issues affect human health, the availability of resources and the quality of the environment.

items.followUp: What is an organ? Give one example of an organ and identify its tissues.

rubric.why: Defines tissue at the cellular level.
rubric.description: A tissue is a group of similar cells that perform the same function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a tissue as similar cells working together for a common function.

rubric.why: Illustrates the tissue level with a valid example and function.
rubric.description: Muscle tissue, for example, is made of cells that contract.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct tissue example and its function.

modelAnswer: At the tissue level, similar cells work together to perform the same function.
For example, muscle tissue is made of cells that contract and bring about movement.

items.followUp: Name the major classes of organic biomolecules and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Defines biomolecules.
rubric.description: Biomolecules are molecules present in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining biomolecules as molecules found in living organisms.

rubric.why: Classifies biomolecules into the two broad groups and identifies their distinction.
rubric.description: Biomolecules are classified as organic and inorganic; organic molecules generally contain carbon, while inorganic examples include water and mineral salts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both groups and giving a suitable distinguishing feature or example.

modelAnswer: Biomolecules are molecules present in living organisms.
They are classified into inorganic biomolecules, such as water and mineral salts, and organic biomolecules, such as carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.
Organic biomolecules generally contain carbon, while inorganic biomolecules include substances such as water and mineral salts.
